Period schedule:

Total: 1 periods · 40 minutes

periods.activity_title: Opening the Play: Pre-reading and Act I Role-Assigned Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.169): identify stringed instruments by first letter
Reflect and Respond (p.169): share personal instrument choice and reasons
Reflect and Respond (p.169): discuss music preference differences across generations

phases.description: Teacher introduces the drama Twin Melodies — playwright, setting, and the fusion-versus-classical conflict at its heart. Students skim the cast list and stage directions for Act I (p.169–174).

Reflect and Respond warm-up: pairs identify stringed instruments by first letter, then share instrument preferences and discuss generation gaps in music taste (Reflect and Respond, p.169 — all three oral prompts).
Role-assigned reading of Act I (p.169–174): Shruti, Iqbal, Avinash, Peter parts assigned; teacher reads stage directions and asides aloud, modelling delivery cues and pauses.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the entry period — keep pre-reading brisk so Act I reading gets at least twenty minutes of class time. Students may struggle with stage directions in brackets; model reading one aloud before assigning roles. The fill-in idiom task (Reflect and Respond, p.170) is left for the next period when students have read the act.

periods.activity_title: Act I Comprehension and Predictive Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.170): complete idiom paragraph — literal vs figurative discussion
Reading for Meaning (p.174): complete Act I table — setting, instruments, dialogues
Check Your Understanding (p.169-174): predict whether Shruti will speak to her father
Check Your Understanding (p.169-174): predict father's likely reaction and reasons

phases.description: Brief recap of Act I plot: teacher elicits who the characters are and what Shruti's dilemma is before moving to exercises.

Reflect and Respond (p.170): pairs complete the idiom fill-in paragraph, then whole-class discussion on literal versus figurative meanings of each phrase — teacher clarifies 'bite the bullet' and 'get the ball rolling' in context.

Reading for Meaning (p.174): students complete the Act I table covering setting details, characters and instruments, and speaker-identification for three dialogues; pairs compare answers, teacher confirms.

Check Your Understanding predictive questions (p.169–174): students write a brief reasoned response to whether Shruti will speak to her father and what his reaction might be; three or four students share aloud, class discusses with reference to Act I evidence.

periods.teacher_notes: Shruti's distress is signalled entirely through subtext in Act I — draw students' attention to what she does NOT say rather than only what she says. The figurative idioms in the fill-in task are all drawn from the play's dramatic register; linking them back to actual dialogue lines deepens comprehension. Acts II and III will be read in the next period.

periods.activity_title: Acts II and III: Role-Assigned Reading and Mid-Play Comprehension

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Meaning (p.178): complete Act II summary — fill correct words from box
Check Your Understanding (p.178): predict whether Nabin will attend rehearsal
Check Your Understanding (p.178): discuss whether Shruti and parents will understand each other

phases.description: Role-assigned reading of Acts II and III (p.175–182): Shruti, Nabin, Leela, Iqbal, Avinash parts assigned; teacher reads stage directions including the unannounced arrival scene and Nabin's foot-tapping moment.

Reading for Meaning (p.178): students complete the Act II summary fill-in (eight blanks from the word box), checking in pairs before teacher confirms answers and highlights the word 'clash' as the thematic key.

Check Your Understanding predictive questions (p.178): students respond briefly to whether Nabin will attend the rehearsal and whether mutual understanding is achievable; brief whole-class share with textual justification.

periods.teacher_notes: Act II is the play's emotional pivot — Nabin's cold dismissal and Leela's quiet rebuke are the moments students most need to sit with. Note that Nabin's parallel history (defying his own family to play violin) is only revealed in Act III; caution students not to jump ahead when doing prediction tasks. The true/false task for Act III will be anchored in the next period.

periods.activity_title: Act III Close Reading and Extract Analysis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.181-182): identify true statements about Act III
Critical Reflection (p.182-183): two extracts — close-reading and paired discussion

phases.description: Quick oral recap of Act III's resolution: teacher asks what changes Nabin's mind and students cite Leela's revelation about his own rebellion, orienting the class to the thematic payoff before close-reading.

Check Your Understanding (p.181–182): pairs work through the six true/false statements about Act III, then class confirms with page-specific evidence for each; teacher flags the subtlety that Nabin did NOT defame the raga notes — a key detail students misread.

Critical Reflection (p.182–183): both extracts worked in sequence — Extract 1 (Shruti/Iqbal dilemma exchange): four sub-questions including multiple-choice, short-answer, fill-in, and short explanation; Extract 2 (Nabin's breakthrough speech): five sub-questions including multiple-choice, fill-in, word-choice, extended inference, and phrase identification; pairs draft answers, whole-class discussion follows each extract.

periods.teacher_notes: The phrase 'each bay, its own wind' in Extract 2 is the play's thematic capstone — ensure students articulate what it means for each artist's unique journey rather than just translating it literally. The extended-answer inference on Shruti's future (Extract 2, sub-question iv) prepares students for the full analytical questions in the next period. Unselected sub-items from earlier Check Your Understanding tasks not revisited here may be used for personal reflection at home.

periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection: Analytical Essay Questions on the Drama

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.184): six analytical questions — title, character arc, theme, conclusion evaluation

homework.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.184): complete remaining extended-answer questions not finished in class

phases.description: Teacher frames the six analytical questions (p.184) as a set: title justification, character perspectives, Nabin's arc, Shruti's internal conflict, conclusion evaluation, and cultural diversity — students note the range of cognitive demands before writing.

Students work individually on the six extended-answer questions; teacher circulates, prompting use of textual evidence and discouraging plot summary in favour of analysis — directing students to specific acts for each question.

Structured share: two or three students read their response to the title-justification question aloud; class offers additions; teacher models how 'Twin Melodies' operates on both the literal (violin + fusion) and symbolic (tradition + modernity) levels.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often conflate plot summary with analysis on questions such as Nabin's character arc — remind them the question asks how his attitude evolves, which requires citing Act I dismissal, Act III foot-tapping, and the final speech as three distinct stages. Questions not completed in class serve as homework reinforcement. This period closes Section A's reading work; Vocabulary and Grammar begins next.

periods.activity_title: Vocabulary and Structures in Context: Dramatic Devices and Grammar

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.184): identify and explain the dramatic device 'aside'
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.185): non-lexical fillers — why used; match fillers to emoticons
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.186): match music-related vocabulary to meanings

phases.description: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.184): teacher reads the 'aside' excerpt aloud; students choose the correct option for what an aside does, then briefly discuss how Shruti's aside in Act III reveals her inner conflict to the audience but not to other characters.

Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.185): class identifies why non-lexical fillers appear in the play's dialogue (to fill gaps while speaking); pairs match 'whew, err, arrgh, hmmm' to four emoticons and share answers, noting the extra filler.

Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.186): music-related vocabulary matching — students work individually to pair 'rhythm, tempo, bass, baritone, cacophony, pitch, scale' with definitions, check in pairs, then teacher connects each term to moments in the play (e.g. Nabin praising Shruti for staying true to the raga's pitch).

periods.teacher_notes: The aside and non-lexical filler tasks together consolidate dramatic-script literacy introduced in the Beyond-the-Text section; connecting them here avoids repetition later. Students frequently confuse 'baritone' (voice range) with 'bass' (lowest tone) — a brief contrast using the characters' voices helps. The phrase-meaning task (p.186: 'drown your individual style', etc.) and reported-speech tasks are anchored in the following period.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.186): write meanings of three play-derived phrases
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.187): identify exclamatory sentences; convert to declarative with 'exclaimed'
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.187): convert six play dialogues to reported speech

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.188): report Asma-Deepa dialogue in indirect speech

phases.description: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.186): students write meanings of 'drown your individual style', 'sense of musicality', and 'go down the drain' based on in-text usage; pairs compare, teacher confirms and links each phrase to the drama's conflict — Nabin's fear that fusion would 'drown' Shruti's classical style.

Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.187): teacher elicits the sentence type for the two play exclamations; students identify them as exclamatory, then individually convert both to declarative sentences using 'exclaimed' or 'exclaimed with (feeling)', removing interjections and exclamatory marks; two or three students read aloud and class refines wording.

Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.187): reported-speech transformation of six play dialogues — teacher models item 1 (already done), students work items 2–6 individually; pairs cross-check tense shifts and pronoun changes; teacher addresses the most common error (forgetting to shift 'are' to 'were') on the board.
Teacher sets homework — the Asma-Deepa reported-speech dialogue (p.188) — and clarifies the four-blank format so students know what is expected before next class.

periods.teacher_notes: Reported speech of exclamatory sentences is a new grammatical territory at this level — students reliably omit 'with wonder/joy/disappointment' modifiers; keep the error-correction phase short but visible on the board. Connecting transformations to actual play lines (Avinash calling Shruti a sensation, Shruti apologising to her mother) keeps the grammar contextually meaningful. The Asma-Deepa dialogue (p.188) is assigned as homework to consolidate the pattern in a fresh context.

periods.activity_title: Yazh Listening Notes and Stress-Intonation Speaking Activity

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.189): listen to yazh description; complete notes in three words or fewer
Speaking Activity (p.189-190): stress and intonation exercise using four lines from the play

phases.description: Listen and Respond warm-up: teacher displays images of several Indian stringed instruments; students silently choose which one they believe could be the yazh — no answers given yet (p.189, pre-listening task).
Teacher reads the yazh transcript aloud (transcript: p.270) as students listen and check their image choice; brief show-of-hands confirmation before proceeding to note-taking.

Listen and Respond (p.189): teacher reads the transcript a second time at moderate pace; students simultaneously complete the structured notes — instrument type, ancient Tamil use, earlier version, stem-tip carving, resonator shape and material, design variety names; pairs cross-check answers, teacher confirms correct completions.

Speaking Activity (p.189–190): teacher models the four play lines with marked stress and intonation; students repeat chorally, then in pairs practise all four lines, experimenting with how shifting stress changes emotional impact (e.g. stressing 'papa' versus 'opinions'); three pairs perform for the class and class gives brief feedback on clarity and expressiveness.

Brief debrief: teacher asks what the yazh listening and the stress-intonation work share — both foreground how sound shapes meaning; students connect this to Nabin's observation about Shruti never losing the raga notes even in fusion performance.

periods.teacher_notes: The yazh transcript (p.270) should be read at a natural pace for the first listening and slightly slower for the note-taking pass — do not rush the design-variety names as students often mishear 'matsya' and 'makara'. For the stress activity, the line 'Each bay, its own wind' is the most thematically rich and the most open to interpretive performance; give pairs a moment to discuss what emotion they are conveying before performing. The self-practice speaking task (p.190, task 2) is left for independent follow-up.

periods.activity_title: Play-Script Writing and Dramatic Convention Exploration

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.169-193): groups of four draft play script from Anuradha story prompt
Learning Beyond the Text (p.192): analyse play-script conventions — no inverted commas, colons, brackets, stage directions

phases.description: Learning Beyond the Text (p.192): teacher projects two or three dialogue excerpts from the play and guides whole-class analysis of the four convention questions — why no inverted commas, where colons appear, what brackets convey, and how stage directions help actors; students respond orally, teacher summarises on board.

Teacher introduces the Writing Task (p.169–193): reads the Anuradha story prompt aloud, assigns groups of four, and reviews the six script-writing tips — rough draft, setting and characters, colon after speaker name, brackets for stage directions, asides, non-lexical fillers, ellipsis for pauses.

Guided writing: groups plan their setting and character list (5 min), then draft a two-scene script collaboratively using the tips as a checklist; teacher circulates, prompting groups to include at least one aside and one non-lexical filler; final 5 minutes each group reads their opening exchange aloud for the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The play-script writing task intentionally mirrors the Anuradha-tabla scenario (father disapproves, mother and brother support) with the structure of the drama just studied — this parallel is worth naming aloud so students draw on Twin Melodies as a model. Remind groups that stage directions must be in brackets and in the present tense, as modelled in the textbook play. Beyond-the-Text tasks on the Recycled Orchestra of Cateura, indigenous instruments, and reading Rigmarole are left as self-study enrichment pointers for interested students.

periods.activity_title: Poem Reading and Appreciation: Metaphors and Poetic Devices

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.194): share music preferences, favourite musicians, and reasons
Reading for Appreciation (p.195): complete poet's diary — fill blanks from poem
Reading for Appreciation (p.195): appreciate poem — device identification, metaphor-to-simile, rhyme scheme, anaphora, message, mood
Critical Reflection (p.196): extract 'Music is the therapy…' — five sub-questions

homework.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.196): five extended-answer questions on poet's attitude and universal appeal

phases.description: Reflect and Respond (p.194): students share their music preferences (vocal or instrumental), name favourite musicians, and give reasons in pairs; two or three pairs report to the class — teacher links the variety of responses to the poem's claim of music's universal appeal.

Teacher reads the poem aloud twice — first for overall mood, second with students following text; students complete the poet's diary fill-in (p.195, six blanks using words from the poem) individually, then verify in pairs.

Reading for Appreciation (p.195): teacher works through all seven sub-questions with the class — students identify the ambiguous meaning of 'moves me', convert each metaphor to a simile, name the ABCB rhyme scheme and its effect, explain the anaphoric repetition of 'Music is…', articulate the poem's message, identify the mood, and cite evidence that the speaker is the poet herself.

Critical Reflection extract (p.196): 'Music is the therapy…' — students answer all five sub-questions individually (fill-in for 'feel blue', identify the happiness line, explain the last line, true/false, central idea multiple-choice); teacher confirms answers and highlights how 'pull through' functions as a phrasal verb — a bridge to Section B's vocabulary work.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's anaphoric 'Music is…' structure is its most distinctive formal feature and students should be able to name it as anaphora and connect it to the meditative tone described in the appreciation summary. When converting metaphors to similes, caution students that 'Music is as an ocean as the shore' is a structural error — model the correct form before they attempt the others. The five extended-answer questions (p.196) are set as homework to free class time for vocabulary and listening work in the final period.

periods.activity_title: Emotion Vocabulary, Phrasal Verbs, and Santoor Listening

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context (p.197): classify emotion words; fill blanks with correct emotion vocabulary
Vocabulary in Context (p.198): match six 'move' phrasal verbs to correct meanings
Listen and Respond (p.199): pre-listen; read questions and guess answers before hearing conversation
Listen and Respond (p.199): listen to santoor conversation; verify and correct guesses

phases.description: Vocabulary in Context (p.197): students classify 'feel blue / lifts my spirits / most cheerful' as positive or negative emotions, then individually fill the four blanks choosing between paired words (nostalgia/elation, despondence/anguish, melancholy/despair, jubilant/euphoric); pairs compare, teacher confirms and briefly explains connotation differences within each pair.

Vocabulary in Context (p.198): teacher explains phrasal verbs using 'pull through' from the poem, then students match six 'move' phrasal verbs (move out, move in, move on, move over, move along, move off) to their meanings from the box; pairs cross-check and teacher confirms.

Listen and Respond pre-listening (p.199): students read all six multiple-choice questions and write their best guesses (relationship, location, instrument, problem, failed solution, final decision) before any audio — teacher clarifies that the purpose is to activate prediction, not to get the right answer.

Teacher reads the santoor conversation transcript aloud (transcript: p.270); students check and correct their pre-listening guesses; brief show-of-hands for each item confirms answers, and teacher connects Jaspreet's santoor dilemma to Shruti's violin dilemma in the drama — a thematic thread across the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: The emotion-vocabulary task (p.197) is intentionally placed after reading the poem so the words 'feel blue' and 'lifts my spirits' are already contextualised — students should not need to look them up. For the 'move' phrasal verb matching, note that 'move on' (to progress) is frequently confused with 'move off' (to start moving) — a brief contrast on the board helps. Section B's writing task (invitation letter, p.200), speaking task (role play, p.200), and beyond-text tasks are unanchored due to the available period count; flag the invitation letter as a worthwhile home exercise and the role play as a potential club or assembly activity.
